openers.env: Carbon never sits still. It moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere, and soil is one of its great holding places. That stored carbon takes two forms: organic matter from plants, animals and microbes, and carbonate minerals. This part of the course follows soil into the wider environment, beginning with the two-way link between soil carbon and climate. A changing climate alters soils and their carbon, and every loss or gain of that carbon alters the climate in turn, with consequences that reach from the frozen Arctic to the world's food supply.
openers.soil-carbon-and-climate: Soil organic matter is about 50% carbon by dry weight, and more carbon sits in soil as carbonate minerals. This chapter asks what happens to that store as the climate changes. Processes that pull carbon from the air and lock it away can slow warming, and so can land and farm practices that stop soils losing carbon and help them build it up. Losses run the other way and feed warming. The chapter ends in the Arctic, where carbon passes from frozen soils to plants, microbes and air, and where the top layer of ground thaws every summer and refreezes every autumn.

soil-env-102.title: The carbon cycle: one element circling through soil, sea and sky
soil-env-102.text: Limestone cliffs and living cells are built partly of the same element. Carbon is the main component of biological compounds and a major part of many rocks. The carbon cycle is the part of Earth's biogeochemical cycles, described in {{ref:soil-fert-140}}, in which carbon moves among living things, soils, rocks, water and the atmosphere. Scientists divide it into reservoirs: the atmosphere, the land's living things and soils, the ocean, sediments and Earth's interior. Chemical, physical, geological and biological processes shift carbon between them. Near Earth's surface, the ocean holds the largest active store. Photosynthesis is the main route by which carbon dioxide leaves the air and enters land and ocean life. Left alone, the flows between air, ocean, land and sediments are fairly balanced, so carbon levels would stay roughly stable. Humans have upset that balance for centuries. They changed land use, and they mined and burned coal, petroleum and gas. By 2020 atmospheric carbon dioxide stood nearly 52% above pre-industrial levels, driving global warming. Today the land and the ocean each absorb about one-quarter of human carbon emissions every year.

soil-env-106.title: Soil carbon, a store three times the atmosphere's
soil-env-106.text: Soils hold about 2,700 gigatons (Gt) of carbon, roughly three times as much as the atmosphere. Soil carbon is the solid carbon stored in soils, and it comes in two forms. About 1550 GtC is organic, from plants, animals and microbes, the material of {{ref:soil-found-045}}. Another 950 GtC is inorganic, held in the carbonate minerals met in {{ref:soil-found-034}}. Peat and wetlands hold a further 150 GtC, and surface plant litter 50 GtC. This store is far from idle. About 60 GtC a year accumulates in soil, and an equal 60 GtC a year is respired back to the air. Photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition set how much carbon stays on land. Soil carbon underpins water holding capacity, nutrient retention and soil structure. It matters for climate too, since soil takes up carbon in the global cycle, and data on it feed global climate models. Those data are inconsistent, with some regions far better covered than others. Human activities have caused a massive loss of soil carbon, yet people could also deliberately return carbon to the soil.

soil-env-116.title: Carbon sinks: places that take in more than they give
soil-env-116.text: During the growing season, land plants pull more carbon from the air than they release. That makes them a carbon sink. A sink is a natural or artificial process that removes a greenhouse gas, or a substance that forms one, from the atmosphere. It takes up more carbon than it releases. Sinks are an important part of the natural carbon cycle. Globally the two most important are vegetation and the ocean, which absorbs carbon through its solubility and biological pumps. Soil is both an important carbon store and an active sink. Artificial sinks lock carbon in building materials or deep underground. No major artificial system yet removes carbon from the atmosphere at large scale. For gases other than CO2, a sink need not store anything. Nitrous oxide, for example, can be reduced to harmless nitrogen gas, N2. Deforestation and industrial agriculture have depleted natural sinks, and this land-use change is one cause of climate change. Keeping and enhancing natural sinks, mainly soils and forests, is therefore important for slowing it.

soil-env-167.title: Climate change mitigation: cutting the gases that warm the planet
soil-env-167.text: Almost 20% of greenhouse gas emissions come from agriculture and forestry. Climate change mitigation, also called decarbonisation, is action to limit the greenhouse gases that cause climate change. It includes conserving energy and replacing fossil fuels with clean energy. Another key measure is managing carbon sinks so they remove more CO2 and store it durably. The 2022 IPCC report calls these land-based AFOLU options and puts their economic potential at 4.2 to 7.4 GtCO2-eq a year. Cutting nitrogen fertilizer use could avoid nitrous oxide equal to 2.77 - 11.48 gigatons of CO2 from 2020 to 2050.

soil-env-212.title: Carbon sequestration: putting carbon away
soil-env-212.text: Turn natural or semi-natural land into cropland, and its soil loses about 30-40% of its organic carbon. Carbon sequestration works in the opposite direction. It is the storing of carbon in a reservoir of the carbon cycle, which limits climate change by reducing carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. It comes in two main types, biological and geological. Biological sequestration, or biosequestration, captures CO2 through living processes such as photosynthesis. Land-use and farming changes that speed it up are called carbon farming. Sequestration is sometimes confused with carbon capture and storage, which separates CO2 from industrial sources and stores it underground or under the sea bed. Biological stores can be temporary, because wildfire, disease, economic pressure and politics can release their carbon again. Mineral sequestration is far more durable, locking carbon in insoluble carbonate salts for thousands to millions of years. In soil, carbon keeps changing after land is cleared until a new equilibrium is reached. Leaving residues, using manure and adding perennial crops, with their larger below-ground biomass, all raise carbon input. Outside permafrost, about 70% of the organic carbon in the upper metre lies deeper down, stabilized by its association with minerals.

soil-env-110.title: Soil carbon and climate: a two-way street
soil-env-110.text: Climate shapes soils, and soils answer back. Changing temperature and moisture alter soil formation. Climate change is therefore likely to affect fertility, salinity, moisture, temperature, organic carbon and aggregation. In return, soil carbon losses or gains alter the climate. Plants fix carbon dioxide into soil, building a pool of around 1500 petagrams (Pg) in the first few metres. Some 20-40% of it lasts more than 100 years. Forest soils are a large part of that pool, and deforestation releases carbon that may markedly raise greenhouse gases in the air. Soil microbes break soil carbon down, and changes in their activity as temperatures rise could add to climate change. Regions respond differently. In polar regions, melting permafrost can open land to more plant growth and carbon uptake. In the tropics, warmer soils lose aggregation and quality. Researchers are looking for ways farming and other human interventions can restore carbon to soils.

soil-env-162.title: How a warming climate makes farming harder
soil-env-162.text: One study linked 1°C of warming to a 3 to 7% fall in global yields of major staple crops. Climate change alters farming in many ways, and most of them make it harder for agriculture to provide global food security. Drought, heat waves and flooding lower crop yields. Climate change is also likely to worsen farming's environmental impacts, by lowering productivity, weakening agrochemicals and increasing soil erosion and pests. The land itself shifts. Sea level rise takes coastal farmland, while thawing frozen ground opens new arable land. Soil fertility and growing seasons change. CO2 fertilization, the extra growth that more carbon dioxide can bring, offsets a small part of the harm. Yet it lowers essential micronutrients in crops and does little for C4 crops like maize. The future extent of soil erosion and groundwater depletion are among the main uncertainties. Farmers can adapt through management practices, agricultural innovation, institutional change and climate-smart agriculture.

soil-env-107.title: Carbon locked in minerals: soil's carbonate store
soil-env-107.text: In arid and semi-arid lands, most soil carbon is not organic at all. It is soil inorganic carbon: carbon held as minerals, mainly carbonates such as calcite and dolomite. Some carbonate comes ready-made from bedrock or parent material. Some forms in place in the soil and is called pedogenic carbonate. It arises from the weathering of parent material, or from soil minerals reacting with CO2 from the air. Worldwide, inorganic carbon makes up about 950 GtC, roughly a third of all soil carbon. The store can be undone. The reactions are reversible: when carbonate meets hydrogen ions from acids, as it does in soils, it forms water and releases CO2 back to the air.

soil-env-108.title: Soil organic carbon, built from roots, leaves and dead microbes
soil-env-108.text: The remains of dead microbes, called microbial necromass, can make up 30 to 80% of soil carbon. Microbes cycle it that thoroughly. This is soil organic carbon: the carbon held in soil organic matter, which is about 50% carbon by dry weight. In humid environments most soil carbon takes this form. Its main source is dead plant material arriving as roots, fallen leaves and crop residue, with animal bodies and excreta adding more. Living plants pass 5–20% of the carbon they fix to the soil as root exudates, feeding rhizosphere organisms such as mycorrhizal fungi. Cellulose, starches, proteins and lipids break down fast. Lignin, humus, aggregate-bound organic matter and charcoal persist. Most upland topsoils hold 0.5% to 3.0% organic carbon. Below 0.5% is mostly limited to deserts, and above 12–18% soils are classed as organic soils. Carbon builds up where waterlogging slows decomposition, as in swamps, bogs and marshes. Charcoal and other fire-derived carbon typically supply 5–50% of it, and more than 50% in mollisols, chernozems and terra preta.

soil-env-111.title: Keeping carbon in the ground: land use decides
soil-env-111.text: In the Netherlands, East Anglia, Florida and the California Delta, peatlands have subsided severely. Tillage and drainage exposed their organic matter to oxygen. Managing soil carbon means choosing land and farm practices that avoid such losses of soil organic carbon and build it up. The exchange of carbon between soils and the atmosphere is a significant part of the global carbon cycle, and humans and farming now affect it most. Land-use change such as deforestation has caused substantial losses, though exact amounts are hard to measure. Fire strips soil cover and causes immediate and continuing losses. So does grazing that leaves soil bare, through recovery periods that are too long or too short. Farmers are discouraged from stubble burning and over-cultivation and encouraged to work in organic material such as manure. Raising soil carbon is not simple, though. Soil organisms consume and release carbon, and they become more active when nitrogen fertilizer is added.

soil-env-154.title: Carbon in the deep freeze: the permafrost carbon cycle
soil-env-154.text: Permafrost-affected soils cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they store between 25 and 50% of its soil organic carbon. The permafrost carbon cycle is the Arctic part of the global carbon cycle. Carbon moves from frozen soils to plants, microbes and the air. It returns to permafrost through burial and sedimentation driven by freezing, or cryogenic, processes, while some passes to the ocean and the wider cycle. The cycle includes exchanges of carbon dioxide and methane with the air. It also includes transfers to water as dissolved and particulate carbon, both organic and inorganic. Because permafrost responds slowly to climate, it keeps carbon out of the air for long periods. Radiocarbon dating shows much of it is thousands of years old. Early carbon estimates and climate models often neglected this reservoir, but research on it has grown enormously since the 2000s. Microbial respiration is the main route by which old permafrost carbon re-enters the air. Soil temperature, moisture, nutrients and oxygen set its rate. Minerals can slow the escape. Iron oxides can hold back respiration, and iron and aluminum can adsorb freed carbon, especially in the sandy layers often found over permafrost. Despite the huge stores, the whole pool is unlikely to mobilize, because much permafrost will stay frozen even as thaw deepens.

soil-env-146.title: The active layer, the ground that thaws each summer
soil-env-146.text: In northeastern Siberia, Alaska and Greenland, summer thaws the ground to less than 50 centimetres. In southern Norway and Mongolia it thaws past 600 centimetres. That seasonal skin is the active layer: the top layer of soil in permafrost regions that thaws each summer and freezes again in autumn. In 2018 it averaged about 145 centimetres across the Northern Hemisphere. Soil temperature is steadier at depth than at the surface, so seasonal heating and cooling fade downward. In winter a frost front forms in the soil. In spring and summer the soil thaws from the top down. Where summer heat cannot thaw it completely, permafrost forms. The year-round frozen soil below is the inactive layer, and the boundary is sometimes called the permafrost table. Water cannot drain below the active layer, so permafrost lands tend to be very poorly drained and boggy. Roots cannot grow below it either, which restricts trees over continuous permafrost to shallow-rooted species such as larch.

soil-env-118.title: Why soils hold more carbon than plants and air combined
soil-env-118.text: A tropical field cleared by slash-and-burn stays fertile for only two to three years. Heat and rain are the reason: in tropical and subtropical climates, litter and humus oxidize fast and rain leaches them away. Taken as a whole, though, soils are a short- to long-term carbon store, holding more carbon than all land vegetation and the atmosphere combined. Plant litter and other biomass, charcoal included, build up as soil organic matter. Tougher compounds such as lignin, waxes and terpenoids are retained together as humus. Organic matter accumulates in cold regions such as the boreal forests of North America and the Russian taiga. Grasslands store it mainly in fibrous root mats, and natural grass fires leave stable biochar. Since the 1850s much of the world's grassland has been tilled into cropland, rapidly oxidizing large amounts of soil organic carbon. Methods that markedly raise carbon storage, such as no-till, residue mulching, cover cropping and crop rotation, are called carbon farming.

soil-env-168.title: Soil carbon sequestration: drawing carbon down into the ground
soil-env-168.text: In 2004 Science published a paper on soil carbon sequestration by the scientist profiled in {{ref:soil-hist-026}}. It was the first to report that restoring soil organic matter does two jobs at once. It improves soil health, and it reduces atmospheric CO2. Soil carbon sequestration is that process: drawing carbon dioxide from the air into soil, where plants fix it as organic carbon. It is both a major soil property and an ecosystem service. Farming can deplete soil carbon, but conservation farming can protect it and repair the damage over time. Methods include cover crops, no-till farming, residue mulching and crop rotation. For European soils the best practices are converting arable land to grassland, straw incorporation, reduced tillage, ley cropping and cover crops. Trees exude more carbon below ground than they capture above it, helping build a carbon-rich soil described in {{ref:soil-env-119}}. Biochar retains half the carbon of the biomass it is made from and can endure in soil for thousands of years. The potential is large. Protecting healthy soils and restoring that sponge could remove 7.6 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, more than annual US emissions. The many measures make soil carbon hard to measure and account for. Yet they carry fewer trade-offs than afforestation or BECCS, bioenergy with carbon capture and storage.

soil-env-170.title: Pingos, hills with a heart of ice
soil-env-170.text: John Franklin first described a pingo in 1825. In 1938 Alf Erling Porsild borrowed the Inuvialuit word, meaning conical hill, for scientific use. A pingo is an ice-cored hill, 3–70 m high and 30–1,000 m across, that grows only in permafrost. More than 11,000 exist, the most, 1,350, on the Tuktoyaktuk peninsula. Closed-system pingos form as an infilled lake freezes and squeezes trapped water upward. Open-system pingos are fed by artesian groundwater. Pingos grow a couple of centimetres a year. When the ice core melts, they collapse into depressions that show permafrost once existed.

soil-env-139.title: Permafrost thaw: the frozen ground is shrinking
soil-env-139.text: In parts of Northern Alaska, permafrost warmed by up to 3 °C between the early 1980s and the mid-2000s. Permafrost thaw is the warming and thawing of permafrost under climate change, seen as a thickening active layer and shrinking frozen ground. Globally, permafrost warmed by about 0.3 °C between 2007 and 2016, more where it is continuous than where it is patchy. In the Russian European North it warmed by up to 2 °C from 1970 to 2020. The active layer has thickened too. Its average rose from about 127 centimetres to about 145 centimetres between 2000 and 2018, roughly 0.65 centimetres a year. Frozen ground is retreating. In Yukon the zone of continuous permafrost may have moved 100 kilometres poleward since 1899, though accurate records span only 30 years. Model projections, process understanding and evidence from past climates make it virtually certain that permafrost will keep shrinking as climate warms. The volume of permafrost in the upper 3 m is expected to fall by about 25% per 1 °C of global warming.

soil-env-130.title: Continuous to isolated: grading permafrost by coverage
soil-env-130.text: About 15% of the Northern Hemisphere's ice-free land sits directly on permafrost, yet 22% lies within a permafrost zone. The difference comes from how the zones work. Permafrost zones divide frozen regions by how much of the land is underlain by permafrost. In the continuous zone 90%–100% is, in the discontinuous zone 50%–90%, and in the sporadic zone 10%–50%. Isolated patches cover 10% or less. Soil scientists abbreviate the continuous zone CPZ, the extensive discontinuous zone DPZ and the sporadic zone SPZ. Temperature sets the pattern. Permafrost usually forms wherever mean annual air temperature is below freezing. Humid boreal forests are the exception, because snow insulates the ground there. Where the mean annual soil surface temperature lies between −5 and 0 °C, permafrost usually stays discontinuous, forming only in sheltered spots. Below −5 °C, not even a slope's aspect, the direction it faces, can thaw it, and a continuous zone forms.

soil-env-112.title: What extra soil carbon does for a whole catchment
soil-env-112.text: Raising soil carbon does more than store carbon. Carbon catchment health names those wider benefits, for the soil and for its catchment, the land that drains to a waterway. More stable aggregates resist erosion and sedimentation, and soils that keep their strength when wet are less prone to mass movement. Nutrients and sediment stay in the soil instead of leaching or washing into waterways. Greater water holding capacity cuts overland flow and keeps water available to plants. The benefits are hard to quantify, because natural resource systems are complex and soil health is open to interpretation.

soil-env-113.title: Counting the carbon: how countries track soil stocks
soil-env-113.text: One model puts the organic carbon in the topsoil of EU farmland at 17.63 Gt. Figures like that come from soil carbon monitoring: estimating organic carbon stocks and their changes by field survey and modelling. Climate reporting requires it. Under the UN climate convention, countries report changes in five carbon stores, soil carbon among them, following IPCC good practice guidance. Tanzania, with the FAO, runs a forest soil carbon programme that combines survey and modelling. For Europe, the European Soil Database gives the most consistent data. Australian farm soils, typically 1.6–4.6% carbon today, may once have held twice as much.
